meta.titre: Thermodynamics: First Law, Gas Processes and Cycles

sections.contenu_markdown: A diesel engine in a Douala bus burns fuel to push pistons, yet more than half of the energy in each litre leaves through the exhaust and radiator as heat. A refrigerator in a Limbe fish shop does the opposite: it moves heat from the cold inside to the warm shop, and it needs electricity to do so. Thermodynamics explains both with two laws, one about the conservation of energy and one about the direction in which processes happen. The GCE Advanced Level paper asks you to apply the first law to gas processes, to read pressure-volume diagrams and to state what the second law forbids.

items: The equation of state of an ideal gas is $pV=nRT$ with $T$ in kelvin and $R=8.31\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$.

Work done by a force is force times displacement, so a gas at pressure $p$ exerting force $pA$ on a piston of area $A$ does work $p\,\Delta V$ when its volume changes by $\Delta V$ at constant pressure.
Temperature in kelvin is the temperature in degrees Celsius plus $273$.
Energy is conserved: it can be transferred or transformed but not created or destroyed.

sections.titre: First law, gas processes and the second law
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Internal energy** $U$ is the sum of the random kinetic and potential energies of the molecules of a system. For an ideal gas the molecules do not attract one another, so $U$ is only the random kinetic energy and depends on temperature alone; for $n$ moles of a monatomic ideal gas $U=\tfrac{3}{2}nRT$. Heat and work are two ways of changing $U$, and neither is stored in the system.

**First law of thermodynamics.** The heat supplied to a system equals the increase in its internal energy plus the work done by the system on its surroundings:
$$Q=\Delta U+W$$
Here $Q$ is positive when heat flows into the gas and $W$ is positive when the gas does work by expanding. (Some books define $W$ as work done **on** the gas and write $\Delta U=Q+W$. State which you are using.)

**Work done by a gas.** At constant pressure $W=p\,\Delta V$. For any change, $W$ is the area under the curve on a graph of $p$ against $V$, and it is negative if the gas is compressed. Around a closed cycle, the net work done by the gas is the **area enclosed** by the loop, and since $U$ returns to its starting value, $\Delta U=0$ so net heat absorbed equals net work done.

**Special changes of an ideal gas.**

| Change | Condition | Consequence of $Q=\Delta U+W$ |
|---|---|---|
| isothermal | $T$ constant | $\Delta U=0$, so $Q=W$ |
| isobaric | $p$ constant | $W=p\,\Delta V$ |
| isochoric | $V$ constant | $W=0$, so $Q=\Delta U$ |
| adiabatic | $Q=0$ | $\Delta U=-W$: expansion cools the gas, compression heats it |

For a reversible adiabatic change, $pV^{\gamma}=\text{constant}$ and $TV^{\gamma-1}=\text{constant}$, where $\gamma=C_p/C_V$ is $\tfrac{5}{3}$ for a monatomic gas.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a closed cycle on a $p$-$V$ graph is given, or efficiency is asked.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
A heat engine takes heat $Q_H$ from a hot source, does net work $W$, and rejects heat $Q_C$ to a cold sink, so $W=Q_H-Q_C$. Its efficiency is
$$\eta=\frac{W}{Q_H}=1-\frac{Q_C}{Q_H}$$
Work out $Q$ for each stage of the cycle, add only the positive values to find $Q_H$, and use the enclosed area for $W$ as a check. The efficiency is always below $1$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to state the second law, to say which processes are possible, or to discuss entropy.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Two equivalent statements: (Clausius) heat does not flow from a colder to a hotter body of its own accord, with no work done; (Kelvin-Planck) it is impossible for a device working in a cycle to take heat from a single reservoir and convert **all** of it into work. Natural processes have a preferred direction because the **entropy** of an isolated system never decreases: it increases in any natural (irreversible) process and stays constant only in an ideal reversible one. A refrigerator moves heat from cold to hot, but only because work is done on it.

sections.enonce_markdown: Two moles of a monatomic ideal gas are heated at a constant pressure of $1.00\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$ from $300\ \mathrm{K}$ to $400\ \mathrm{K}$. Take $R=8.31\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$. Calculate (a) the work done by the gas, (b) the increase in internal energy, and (c) the heat supplied.

etapes.action: Find the initial and final volumes from the equation of state.
etapes.justification: The work at constant pressure needs the change in volume, and the volume follows from $pV=nRT$ with the temperature in kelvin.

etapes.action: Calculate the work done by the gas.
etapes.justification: The pressure is constant, so the work done by the gas as it expands is $p\,\Delta V$.

etapes.action: Calculate the change in internal energy.
etapes.justification: For a monatomic ideal gas $U=\tfrac{3}{2}nRT$, which depends only on temperature.

etapes.action: Apply the first law to find the heat supplied.
etapes.justification: Heat supplied equals the increase in internal energy plus the work done by the gas.

etapes.action: Check with the molar heat capacity at constant pressure.
etapes.justification: For a monatomic gas $C_p=\tfrac{5}{2}R$, which gives the heat supplied at constant pressure directly.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The gas does $1662\ \mathrm{J}$ of work and its internal energy rises by $2493\ \mathrm{J}$, so $4155\ \mathrm{J}$ of heat must be supplied. Two fifths of the heat becomes work and the rest raises the temperature.

items.erreur_markdown: A gas is compressed adiabatically by a piston that does $300\ \mathrm{J}$ of work on it. I wrote $Q=\Delta U+W$ with $W=+300\ \mathrm{J}$ and $Q=0$, so $\Delta U=-300\ \mathrm{J}$.
items.pourquoi_faux: In $Q=\Delta U+W$ the symbol $W$ is the work done **by** the gas. Compression means work is done on the gas, so $W$ is negative.
items.correction_markdown: $W=-300\ \mathrm{J}$, so $0=\Delta U-300$ and $\Delta U=+300\ \mathrm{J}$. Compressing a gas adiabatically raises its internal energy and its temperature.

items.erreur_markdown: A hot cup of tea contains more heat than a cold one.
items.pourquoi_faux: Heat is energy in transit because of a temperature difference. It is not stored in a body.
items.correction_markdown: The hot tea has more **internal energy**. Heat is the energy transferred between the tea and its surroundings.

items.erreur_markdown: No heat enters the gas in an adiabatic expansion, so its temperature does not change.
items.pourquoi_faux: The gas does work on the piston, and with $Q=0$ this work comes from the internal energy of the gas.
items.correction_markdown: $\Delta U=-W<0$, so the temperature falls. It is the **isothermal** change in which the temperature stays constant.

items.pourquoi_faux: The equation of state holds for the absolute temperature, which is proportional to the mean kinetic energy of the molecules. A value in degrees Celsius gives wrong volumes and pressures.

items.erreur_markdown: The second law says heat can never flow from a cold body to a hot body.
items.pourquoi_faux: A refrigerator does exactly that. The law forbids it happening of its own accord, without work being done.
items.correction_markdown: State the law with the condition: heat does not flow from cold to hot **unaided**; external work is needed, as in a refrigerator or heat pump.

items.enonce_markdown: A gas at a constant pressure of $1.5\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$ expands from $2.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^{3}}$ to $5.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^{3}}$ while $700\ \mathrm{J}$ of heat is supplied to it. Calculate (a) the work done by the gas, (b) the increase in its internal energy, and (c) state what happens to the temperature of the gas if it is ideal.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) At constant pressure $W=p\,\Delta V=1.5\times10^{5}\times(5.0\times10^{-3}-2.0\times10^{-3})=450\ \mathrm{J}$.

(b) By the first law $Q=\Delta U+W$, so $\Delta U=Q-W=700-450=250\ \mathrm{J}$.

(c) $\Delta U$ is positive, and the internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, so the temperature of the gas rises.

**$W=450\ \mathrm{J}$; $\Delta U=250\ \mathrm{J}$; the temperature rises.**

items.enonce_markdown: A monatomic ideal gas is taken round a cycle through four states. State A has $p=2.0\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$ and $V=1.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^{3}}$; state B has $2.0\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$ and $3.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^{3}}$; state C has $1.0\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$ and $3.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^{3}}$; state D has $1.0\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$ and $1.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^{3}}$. The gas goes A to B at constant pressure, B to C at constant volume, C to D at constant pressure and D to A at constant volume. Use $U=\tfrac{3}{2}pV$. (a) Find the net work done by the gas in one cycle. (b) Find the total heat absorbed in one cycle (the sum of the heat taken in during the stages in which heat is absorbed). (c) Calculate the efficiency. (d) Verify the first law for the whole cycle.
items.solution_markdown:
Because $pV=nRT$, the internal energy of the monatomic gas is $U=\tfrac{3}{2}pV$, so each change in $U$ is $\tfrac{3}{2}\Delta(pV)$.

| Stage | $\Delta U$ / J | $W$ by gas / J | $Q=\Delta U+W$ / J |
|---|---|---|---|
| A to B | 600 | 400 | 1000 |
| B to C | -450 | 0 | -450 |
| C to D | -300 | -200 | -500 |
| D to A | 150 | 0 | 150 |

Check on A to B: $\Delta U=1.5\times(2.0\times10^{5}\times3.0\times10^{-3}-2.0\times10^{5}\times1.0\times10^{-3})=600\ \mathrm{J}$ and $W=2.0\times10^{5}\times(3.0\times10^{-3}-1.0\times10^{-3})=400\ \mathrm{J}$.

(a) Net work $=400+0-200+0=200\ \mathrm{J}$, which equals the enclosed area $(2.0\times10^{5}-1.0\times10^{5})\times(3.0\times10^{-3}-1.0\times10^{-3})=200\ \mathrm{J}$.

(b) Heat is absorbed in stages A to B and D to A: $Q_H=1000+150=1150\ \mathrm{J}$.

(c) Efficiency $=\dfrac{W}{Q_H}=\dfrac{200}{1150}=0.174$, about 17.4 percent.

(d) $\sum\Delta U=600-450-300+150=0$ and $\sum Q=1000-450-500+150=200\ \mathrm{J}=W_{net}$, as the first law requires over a complete cycle.

**$W_{net}=200\ \mathrm{J}$; $Q_H=1150\ \mathrm{J}$; efficiency $\approx17.4\%$.**

items.enonce_markdown: A cylinder holds $0.20\ \mathrm{mol}$ of a monatomic ideal gas at $290\ \mathrm{K}$ in a volume of $4.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^{3}}$. The gas is compressed adiabatically and reversibly to one eighth of its volume. Take $R=8.31\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ and $\gamma=\tfrac{5}{3}$. (a) Calculate the final temperature. (b) Calculate the initial and final pressures. (c) Calculate the work done on the gas. (d) Compare with an isothermal compression to the same volume and explain the difference in the final pressure.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) For an adiabatic change of a monatomic gas, $TV^{\gamma-1}=\text{constant}$ with $\gamma=\tfrac{5}{3}$: $T_2=T_1\left(\dfrac{V_1}{V_2}\right)^{2/3}=290\times8^{2/3}=290\times4=1160\ \mathrm{K}$.

(b) Initial pressure $p_1=\dfrac{nRT_1}{V_1}=\dfrac{0.20\times8.31\times290}{4.0\times10^{-3}}=1.20\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$. Using $pV^{\gamma}=\text{constant}$: $p_2=p_1\times8^{5/3}=32\,p_1=3.86\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{Pa}$. Check: $p_2V_2=3.86\times10^{6}\times5.0\times10^{-4}=1928\ \mathrm{J}$, which equals $nRT_2=0.20\times8.31\times1160=1928\ \mathrm{J}$.

(c) No heat enters, so the work done on the gas equals its increase in internal energy: $\Delta U=\tfrac{3}{2}nR\,\Delta T=1.5\times0.20\times8.31\times(1160-290)=2169\ \mathrm{J}$.

(d) For an isothermal compression to the same volume, the work done on the gas would be $nRT\ln8=0.20\times8.31\times290\times\ln8=1002\ \mathrm{J}$ and the final pressure would be only $8\,p_1=9.64\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$. In the adiabatic case the work done on the gas stays inside it as internal energy and raises the temperature, so the final pressure is higher and more work is required.

**$T_2=1160\ \mathrm{K}$; $p_2=3.86\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{Pa}$; work done on the gas $=2169\ \mathrm{J}$.**

items_markdown: The first law is $Q=\Delta U+W$, with $W$ the work done by the gas: heat supplied becomes either extra internal energy or work done on the surroundings.
At constant pressure $W=p\,\Delta V$; on a $p$-$V$ graph the work is the area under the curve, and the net work in a cycle is the enclosed area.
Isothermal: $\Delta U=0$. Isochoric: $W=0$. Adiabatic: $Q=0$, so $\Delta U=-W$ and $pV^{\gamma}=\text{constant}$; use kelvin in $pV=nRT$.
Over a complete cycle $\Delta U=0$, so net heat absorbed equals net work; efficiency is $\eta=W/Q_H=1-Q_C/Q_H<1$.
The second law: heat does not flow unaided from cold to hot, no cyclic engine turns all the heat from one source into work, and the entropy of an isolated system never decreases.
